text.p: Department store operator Harris Scarfe Ltd, which has bucked the weak sales trend affecting other major retailers, is expecting firm sales growth through to the end of fiscal 1996/97 and planning aggressive expansion.

In an interview with Reuters, managing director Ron Baker said trading for February was up 3.2 percent on a store for store basis on 1996 and he anticipated it "hovering about 3-3.5 percent" for the rest of the financial year.

Sales were up 23.5 percent for the first eight trading days of March, slightly above budget and, although they would come down with the loss of three trading days over Easter, average gross profit margins were showing a good lift to 31-32 percent from December/January sale levels of around 30 percent, he said.

Harris Scarfe, with nine stores in South Australia, eight in Tasmania, three in Victoria and three in Western Australia, reported a 25 percent rise in net profit for the six months to January 31 to A$5.37 million, already beating the 1995/96's A$4.6 million full year result.
"Whether we can hold the 25 percent (throughout 1996/97) remains to be seen, but (the full year result) will be significantly ahead of last year," Baker said.
With new stores operating through the period, the company achieved a 15.6 percent rise in group sales in the first half to A$123.6 million, up 4.2 percent on a like for like basis.
Baker said the strong performance for the first days of March reflected effective catalogue promotions not held the previous year, but he also detected a general improvement.
"We have not felt (the slump) as badly as the others, but clearly I believe there is a pick-up (occurring)," he said.
In the longer-term, Baker said the closure of David Jones Ltd's John Martin's store in Adelaide's Rundle Mall in February 1998 would be "an absolute bonanza" for his group.

Harris Scarfe, originally a hardware-homeware business, repositioned itself through the 1980s with the arrival of discount department stores like Coles Myer Ltd's K-Mart and Target and the move upmarket by Myer and Grace Brothers.

Filling the gap in the middle market rangE, the group in the last three years haD dramatically grown through acquisition and mergers from its major flagship storE in Adelaide city and affiliates in Tasmania to opening its 24th store next month.

Baker said the group planned to open four stores a year, aiming at 10 stores in Western Australia and 15-20 in Victoria, before examining plans for further expansion to New South Wales and Queensland.
"There is no doubt the company can be a good 40-50 store chain operation just concentrating on those four States."

Baker said growth was most likely to come through new store openings, mostly in suburban or regional locations, with few acquisition opportunities remaining in Australia and the company having no interest in picking up specialist retail chains.
Moves overseas were also not under consideration. "I had a phone call recently from New Zealand and I told them we have a lot to do here before we even think of going offshore," he said.

As well as expanding interstate, Harris Scarfe was also introducing new categories to its stores, including music, electronic games, and toys, while one of its traditional businesses, hardware, now was being phased out, Baker said.

The most successful categories currently were men's and women's fashion, electrical, and manchester, with big growth also from homeware, sporting goods, outdoor casual living and furnishing fabrics, he said.
Despite signs of a retail pickup, Baker said he did not anticipate seeing in his working career a return to the boom years of the 1980s.
"I do not think there is ever going to be an easy road to retailing again, if there was one in the past," he said.
